routes.label: Count exponent choices and minimize the lcm

question: There are exactly \(77{,}000\) ordered quadruples \((a,b,c,d)\) such that \(\gcd(a,b,c,d)=77\) and \(\text{lcm}(a,b,c,d)=n.\) What is the smallest possible value of \(n?\)
solution:
Assume, as intended, that \(a,b,c,d\) are positive integers. Since their gcd is \(77\), write
\[
(a,b,c,d)=77(u,v,w,t),\qquad m=\frac n{77}.
\]
This is a one-to-one correspondence with positive ordered quadruples having gcd \(1\) and lcm \(m\). We seek the smallest such \(m\). The case \(m=1\) gives only the quadruple \((1,1,1,1)\), so \(m>1\).

Consider a prime whose exponent in \(m\) is \(e\ge1\). Its exponents in \(u,v,w,t\) must lie between \(0\) and \(e\). Their minimum must be \(0\), to make the gcd \(1\), and their maximum must be \(e\), to give the required lcm. There are \((e+1)^4\) unrestricted exponent choices. Subtract the \(e^4\) choices missing \(0\) and the \(e^4\) choices missing \(e\), then restore the \((e-1)^4\) choices missing both. The allowed count is
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(e)&=(e+1)^4-2e^4+(e-1)^4\\
&=12e^2+2=2(6e^2+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Choices for different primes are independent. Unique prime factorization ensures that these choices produce every eligible ordered quadruple exactly once, so their counts multiply.

Each \(f(e)\) contains exactly one factor of \(2\), since \(6e^2+1\) is odd. As
\[
77000=2^3\cdot5^3\cdot7\cdot11,
\]
there must be exactly three distinct primes in \(m\). Each contributes at least \(f(1)=14\). If any exponent were at least \(6\), the count would be at least
\[
f(6)\cdot14^2=434\cdot196=85064>77000.
\]
Thus every exponent is at most \(5\). The possible contributions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(1)&=14=2\cdot7,\\
f(2)&=50=2\cdot5^2,\\
f(3)&=110=2\cdot5\cdot11,\\
f(4)&=194=2\cdot97,\\
f(5)&=302=2\cdot151.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last two introduce prime factors absent from \(77000\), so they are impossible. Exactly one contribution must be \(14\) to supply the single factor of \(7\), and exactly one must be \(110\) to supply the factor of \(11\). The remaining contribution is \(50\). Hence the three exponents are \(3,2,1\).

To minimize the number, larger exponents must go on smaller primes. Indeed, if \(p<q\) and \(e>f\), then
\[
\frac{p^e q^f}{p^f q^e}
=\left(\frac pq\right)^{e-f}<1.
\]
Using the three smallest primes therefore gives the universal lower bound
\[
m\ge2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5=360.
\]
This value attains the required count because \(110\cdot50\cdot14=77000\). Consequently,
\[
n=77\cdot360=\boxed{27720},
\]
which is choice \(\text{D}\) under the positive-integer assumption.

The domain qualification matters. If arbitrary signed integers were allowed, every quadruple with positive lcm would have \(16\) independent sign choices, so its total count would be divisible by \(16\). But \(77000\) is not divisible by \(16\). If zeros are allowed and the lcm is defined to be zero, the quadruples \((0,77,77t,77)\), for positive integers \(t\), already give infinitely many possibilities. Thus the displayed statement needs the intended positive-integer convention.
